title: Microbots That Carry Medicine to a Clot
paragraphs: When a blood clot blocks an artery, every minute counts. Depending on where it gets stuck, a clot can cause a stroke, a heart attack or a blockage in the lungs. Clot-dissolving drugs already exist, but delivering them is harder than it sounds. Normally the drug is released through a catheter and the bloodstream carries it forward. Yet when the clot itself has stopped the flow, the drug can only spread slowly, which wastes precious time.

Researchers at ETH Zurich believe they have found a way around this problem. Their microbots are oval grains of a sugar-based gel, roughly the size of red blood cells, with tiny iron oxide particles lined up inside them. Because of this arrangement, each bot turns like a compass needle when a rotating magnetic field is applied from outside the body. Released near the clot together with the drug, the bots tumble along the vessel wall in a series of flips. This motion pushes and pulls the surrounding blood, creating small currents that carry the medicine to its target.

In channels designed to imitate blood vessels, the drug dissolved clots six times faster when the bots were moving. In pigs, the area where blood flow returned after thirty minutes was twice as large as with the drug alone. Even so, the results have not yet passed peer review, and the team says longer safety studies in animals must come before any trials in patients.
